title: Docker & Kubernetes Essentials
subtitle: Weeks 23-25: package and run services anywhere
description: Containerise applications and run them on a cluster: images vs containers, writing Dockerfiles, volumes and networking, Docker Compose for multi-service stacks, then Kubernetes pods, deployments, services, config, storage and Helm.

lessons.title: Images and Containers
lessons.body:
A **container** is a running process that believes it has the whole machine to itself. It is isolated using Linux namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (what it can use), but it shares the host kernel — that is why containers start in milliseconds while a virtual machine boots an entire operating system.

An **image** is the read-only template; a container is a running instance of it. Images are built in **layers**: each instruction adds a layer, and unchanged layers are cached and shared between images, so pulling your app only downloads what is new.

Images live in a **registry** such as Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry. They are named `registry/namespace/name:tag`, for example `nginx:1.27` or `ghcr.io/acme/api:v2`.

```
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx:1.27   # start, detached, publish a port
docker ps                                         # running containers
docker ps -a                                      # include stopped ones
docker logs web                                   # stdout/stderr of PID 1
docker exec -it web sh                            # shell inside the container
docker stop web && docker rm web                  # stop, then remove
docker images                                     # local images
docker pull postgres:16 && docker push myimage    # move images via a registry
```

Container filesystem changes vanish when the container is removed unless you use a volume (Lesson 3). Treat containers as disposable: stop them, throw them away, and start a fresh one from the image.

exercises.prompt: What is the relationship between an image and a container?
options: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance of it
A container is a template; an image is a running copy
They are two names for the same thing
An image only exists inside a running container
exercises.hint: One is the recipe, the other is the cake you can start and stop.
exercises.explain: You build an image, then create one or more containers from it.

exercises.prompt: Why do containers usually start faster than virtual machines?
options: They share the host kernel instead of booting a full operating system
They do not use any isolation
They always run without a filesystem
They are written in a faster language
exercises.hint: Think about what a VM has to boot that a container does not.
exercises.explain: Containers are isolated processes on the host kernel, so there is no guest OS to boot.

exercises.prompt: Write the docker run flag pair that publishes host port 8080 to container port 80
exercises.hint: The short flag is -p, and the order is host:container.
exercises.explain: -p 8080:80 maps host port 8080 to port 80 inside the container.

exercises.prompt: Put the typical container lifecycle commands in the correct order
exercises.explain: Pull the image, run a container, work inside it, stop it, then remove it.
exercises.hint: You fetch the image before you can run it, and clean up last.

lessons.title: The Dockerfile
lessons.body:
A **Dockerfile** is a recipe that builds an image. Instructions run top to bottom, and each one creates a layer.

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

`FROM` sets the base image. `WORKDIR` sets the directory used by later instructions and the container. `COPY` brings files in. `RUN` executes a command *at build time* and bakes the result into a layer. Copying `package*.json` before `COPY . .` lets Docker reuse the cached dependency layer when only your source changes.

`CMD` gives the default command, which the user can override (`docker run img bash`). `ENTRYPOINT` sets a fixed executable, with `CMD` supplying default arguments — use ENTRYPOINT for tools and CMD for apps. Prefer the **exec form** (`["node","server.js"]`) so signals reach your process for a clean shutdown.

**Multistage builds** keep images small by compiling in one stage and copying only the artefacts into the final stage:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
```

Put the lines that change least at the top, and add a `.dockerignore` so `node_modules` and `.git` stay out of the build context.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?
options: RUN executes at build time; CMD sets the default command at container start
RUN sets the default command; CMD runs at build time
They are identical
RUN only copies files; CMD only installs packages
exercises.hint: One bakes a layer into the image, the other starts the process.
exercises.explain: RUN runs during the build and is baked in; CMD declares what runs when the container starts.

exercises.prompt: When would you use ENTRYPOINT instead of CMD?
options: When the container should always run one fixed executable
When you want the default command to be easily overridden
When you need to set environment variables
When you need to install packages
exercises.hint: One of them is hard to override.
exercises.explain: ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD (which users can override) supplies its default arguments.

exercises.prompt: Write a small Dockerfile for a Node.js app whose entry point is `server.js` and which listens on port 3000. Use an official Node base image, set a working directory, copy the app in, expose the port, and start the app with an exec-form command.

patterns.m: start FROM an official Node base image
start the app with an exec-form CMD or ENTRYPOINT

exercises.solution:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
exercises.explain: Order matters: copy the package manifest and install dependencies before copying source, so Docker caches the dependency layer.
exercises.hint: FROM → WORKDIR → COPY → RUN → COPY → EXPOSE → CMD.

exercises.prompt: Put these Dockerfile instructions into a sensible build order
exercises.explain: Base, directory, dependency manifest, install, then source and start command — this maximises layer caching.
exercises.hint: Install dependencies before copying the rest of the source.

lessons.title: Volumes, Networks and Configuration
lessons.body:
Containers are ephemeral, so data that must survive belongs in a **volume**. Docker offers two kinds of mount:

- A **named volume** (`docker volume create dbdata` then `-v dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) is a Docker-managed directory, ideal for databases.
- A **bind mount** (`-v $(pwd)/src:/app/src`) points at a folder on the host, ideal for live-reloading source during development.

```
docker volume create dbdata
docker run -d -v dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
docker run -d -v $(pwd)/html:/usr/share/nginx/html nginx
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --network appnet --name db postgres:16
docker run -d --network appnet --name api -e DB_HOST=db app-demo
docker exec api env | grep DB_
```

On a user-defined **bridge network**, containers reach each other by **name**: the `api` container connects to `db:5432` because Docker's embedded DNS resolves `db` to its IP. This is why the hostname is a service name, not `localhost`. The default bridge does *not* provide this name resolution, so always create your own network.

Configuration travels as **environment variables** with `-e KEY=value` (or `--env-file`). Keep secrets out of images and out of your shell history.

`-p 8080:80` **publishes** a container port to the host. Without `-p`, other containers on the same network can still reach it, but your laptop cannot.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of mount is best for a database's data directory in production?
options: A named volume
A bind mount to your home folder
No mount; keep data in the container
A mount to /tmp
exercises.hint: Docker manages it and it survives container removal.
exercises.explain: Named volumes are Docker-managed and persist independently of the container, which is right for databases.

exercises.prompt: On a user-defined bridge network, how does the api container reach the db container?
options: By the container name db, resolved by Docker's DNS
By connecting to localhost:5432
By the host's public IP address
It cannot; containers are always isolated
exercises.hint: Service names become hostnames.
exercises.explain: Docker's embedded DNS on a user-defined network resolves container names, so api connects to db:5432.

exercises.prompt: Write the docker run flag pair that publishes host port 5432 to container port 5432
exercises.hint: Use -p with host:container.
exercises.explain: -p 5432:5432 exposes Postgres on the host so tools on your machine can connect.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of wiring two containers together in order
items: Create a network with docker network create appnet
Start the database container on that network with a name
Start the app container on the same network
Connect from the app using the database's container name
exercises.explain: A shared user-defined network plus names gives you working service discovery.
exercises.hint: Network first, then both containers on it.

lessons.title: Docker Compose
lessons.body:
**Docker Compose** describes a multi-service stack in one YAML file and brings it up with one command. It is the standard way to run "my app plus its database" locally.

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  dbdata:
```

Each key under `services` becomes a container, and Compose puts them all on one network where service names are hostnames — so `api` reaches Postgres at `db:5432`.

```
docker compose up -d        # build, create and start in the background
docker compose ps           # status
docker compose logs -f api  # follow one service's logs
docker compose exec api sh  # shell into a running service
docker compose down         # stop and remove (named volumes kept)
docker compose down -v      # also delete named volumes
```

`depends_on` controls **start order**, not readiness — Postgres accepts connections a few seconds after it starts. The `condition: service_healthy` form, paired with a `healthcheck`, removes that race so the API does not crash on boot.

exercises.prompt: What does depends_on actually guarantee?
options: Start order only, not that the dependency is ready
That the dependency is fully healthy before starting
Network isolation between services
Automatic backups
exercises.hint: Starting a container and being ready to accept connections are different events.
exercises.explain: depends_on orders startup; use a healthcheck with condition: service_healthy to wait for readiness.

exercises.prompt: Write the command that builds and starts the whole stack in the background
exercises.hint: compose, then up, then detached.
exercises.explain: docker compose up -d builds images, creates the network, and starts every service detached.

exercises.prompt: In the compose file, how does the api service address the database?
options: By the hostname db, the service name
By localhost
By the container ID
exercises.hint: Compose registers each service name on the shared network.
exercises.explain: The service name db is a DNS name on the Compose network, so the URL uses @db:5432.

exercises.prompt: Put a typical Compose workflow in the correct order
exercises.explain: Describe the stack, start it, observe logs, then tear it down.
exercises.hint: You write the file before you start anything.

lessons.title: Kubernetes: Pods, Deployments and Services
lessons.body:
**Kubernetes** (K8s) runs containers across a **cluster** of **nodes**. You declare the desired state in YAML and controllers work to make reality match it — the reconcile loop.

- A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage. Pods are cattle, not pets; they are recreated, never repaired.
- A **Deployment** manages Pods through a ReplicaSet, keeping the chosen number running and performing **rolling updates**.
- A **Service** gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP that load-balances across Pods, whose IPs keep changing.

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml     # create or update from a file
kubectl get pods                      # what is running
kubectl get deployments               # desired vs ready replicas
kubectl describe pod api-7c9f         # events — first stop when a pod is stuck
kubectl logs api-7c9f -c api          # container logs
kubectl exec -it api-7c9f -- sh       # shell inside a pod
kubectl scale deployment api --replicas=5
kubectl rollout status deployment/api
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api   # roll back a bad release
```

A minimal Deployment sets `replicas`, a `selector`, and a pod template with the container `image`, `ports` and resource `requests`/`limits`. A Service of `type: ClusterIP` is internal; `LoadBalancer` or an Ingress exposes it to the internet.

When debugging, read `kubectl describe` events before logs: `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff` and `OOMKilled` are the usual suspects.

exercises.prompt: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
options: A Pod
A Deployment
A Service
A Node
exercises.hint: It wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace.
exercises.explain: A Pod is the smallest unit; Deployments manage Pods and Services expose them.

exercises.prompt: What does a Kubernetes Service provide?
options: A stable DNS name and IP that load-balance across Pods
Persistent disk storage
Container images in a registry
A single physical server
exercises.hint: Pod IPs come and go, so you need something stable in front of them.
exercises.explain: A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and balances traffic across the matching Pods.

exercises.prompt: Write the kubectl command that lists all Pods in the current namespace
exercises.hint: get, then the resource, then optional short name.
exercises.explain: kubectl get pods lists Pods with their status and age.

exercises.prompt: Put this Pod debugging flow in the correct order
items: kubectl get pods to spot the unhealthy Pod
kubectl describe pod to read the events
kubectl logs to read the container output
Fix the manifest and kubectl apply again
exercises.explain: Find it, describe it for events, read its logs, then fix and re-apply.
exercises.hint: Describe shows events; logs show application output.

lessons.title: Kubernetes Configuration and Storage
lessons.body:
Hard-coding a database URL or an API key into an image is a security and portability problem. Kubernetes separates **configuration** from the container.

A **ConfigMap** holds non-sensitive key/value data; a **Secret** holds sensitive data (base64-encoded, and ideally encrypted at rest). Both can be injected as environment variables or mounted as files.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/api:v2
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: api-config
        - secretRef:
            name: api-secret
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 500m
          memory: 256Mi
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
```

**Requests** are what the scheduler reserves; **limits** cap usage. Exceed a memory limit and the kernel kills the container — `OOMKilled`.

**Probes** keep traffic away from unhealthy Pods. A `readinessProbe` removes a Pod from the Service until it passes; a `livenessProbe` restarts it.

Pod filesystems are ephemeral. A **PersistentVolumeClaim** asks for storage, and Kubernetes binds it to a **PersistentVolume** (often provisioned by a cloud **StorageClass**). The Pod mounts the claim by name, so the data outlives the Pod.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
options: A ConfigMap is for non-sensitive data; a Secret is for sensitive data
A ConfigMap stores files; a Secret stores images
A Secret is unencrypted; a ConfigMap is encrypted
They are interchangeable with no difference
exercises.hint: Think about credentials versus ordinary settings.
exercises.explain: ConfigMaps hold plain configuration; Secrets hold sensitive values and should be encrypted at rest.

exercises.prompt: What does a readinessProbe control?
options: Whether a Pod receives traffic from its Service
Whether a Pod is ever restarted
The CPU limit of the Pod
The image pull policy
exercises.hint: It gates traffic, not restart.
exercises.explain: Until the readinessProbe passes, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints; livenessProbe handles restarts.

exercises.prompt: Which Kubernetes object requests persistent storage that a Pod can mount? (give the full name)
exercises.hint: It is the claim, not the volume itself.
exercises.explain: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage and binds to a PersistentVolume, outliving the Pod.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of giving a Pod persistent storage in the correct order
items: Reference that claim as a volume in the Pod spec
Mount the volume into the container at a path
The data survives when the Pod is replaced
exercises.explain: Claim, reference, mount, persist — the claim is decoupled so data outlives the Pod.
exercises.hint: You request storage with a claim before you mount it.

lessons.title: Helm and Managed Kubernetes
lessons.body:
Writing YAML for every environment by hand does not scale. **Helm** is the package manager for Kubernetes: a **chart** is a folder of templated manifests, and **values** fill in the blanks.

```bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo postgresql
helm install mydb bitnami/postgresql -f values.yaml
helm upgrade mydb bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret
helm list
helm rollback mydb 1
helm uninstall mydb
helm template mydb bitnami/postgresql   # render locally without installing
```

A chart has `Chart.yaml` (metadata), `values.yaml` (defaults), and `templates/` containing files with `{{ .Values.image.tag }}` placeholders. You override defaults with `-f prod-values.yaml` or `--set`. Helm tracks each install as a **release**, so `helm rollback` returns to a previous revision — far faster than re-applying manifests by hand.

**Managed Kubernetes** removes control-plane operations. AWS **EKS**, Google **GKE** and Azure **AKS** run the API server and etcd for you; you manage node pools and workloads. All three provide a `kubeconfig`, so plain `kubectl` works unchanged.

For local development, **kind** (Kubernetes in Docker) and **minikube** spin up a single-node cluster on your laptop:

```bash
kind create cluster --name dev
kubectl cluster-info
kind delete cluster --name dev
```

Learn on kind, ship on EKS — the manifests are the same.

exercises.prompt: What is a Helm chart?
options: A package of templated Kubernetes manifests with default values
A running container image
A cloud provider's Kubernetes service
A type of Kubernetes Secret
exercises.hint: It is the unit you install and upgrade.
exercises.explain: A chart packages templated manifests plus values, and Helm installs it as a release.

exercises.prompt: What does helm rollback do?
options: Returns a release to a previous revision
Deletes the cluster
Downloads a new chart version
Reverts your Git repository
exercises.hint: Helm remembers each install and upgrade as a numbered release.
exercises.explain: Helm tracks releases as revisions, so rollback restores an earlier known-good state quickly.

exercises.prompt: Write the helm command that renders a chart locally without installing it (chart reference: bitnami/postgresql, release name mydb)
exercises.hint: Helm has a command named after rendering templates.
exercises.explain: helm template renders the manifests to stdout so you can review them before installing.

exercises.prompt: Put a Helm workflow in the correct order
items: helm repo add to register a chart repository
helm install to deploy a release
helm rollback if the upgrade goes wrong
exercises.explain: Add the repo, install, upgrade, and roll back if needed — all tracked as revisions.
exercises.hint: You must add the repository before you can install from it.
